title: Time Dilation
text:
Thursday’s exit ticket


“The train observer only thinks the strikes weren’t simultaneous — she just received the light at different times.”


Two of your answers — two procedures, one verdict:


Correct the signal

“Frame calculations subtract the light travel time… the events actually occurred at different times in her frame.”


Ask the lattice

“She is using a latticework of synchronised clocks… she checks the records of the strikes.”



She is not fooled — and today that starts costing time itself.

title: Time Dilation
text:
The question we owe L03









L03: “Why not synchronize by carrying one clock over?”

Because moving a clock changes what it reads. Today: by exactly how much.

title: Time Dilation
text:
What a clock actually measures










Proper time \(\Delta\tau\): the time between two events read off one clock that is present at both.

title: Time Dilation
section: The most honest clock in physics
text: The most honest clock in physics

title: Time Dilation
text:
The light clock, live — predict first
Two identical light clocks. One sits still; one flies past at \(0.8c\). Both photons do exactly \(c\) — that is not negotiable.
In your notebook, before anything runs:

When her clock shows 6 ticks, what does yours show — more, fewer, or the same? Commit — with a number if you dare, and one line of why.
We then slide the speed up toward \(0.95c\). What happens to her photon’s speed — and what does its path do instead?

title: Time Dilation
text:
What you just watched, frozen









Same mirrors, same photon — but in your frame the photon travels a zigzag, and the zigzag is longer than the straight bounce.


Postulate 2: the photon does \(c\) for you too. Longer path at the same speed → the moving clock’s tick takes longer.

title: Time Dilation
text:
The geometry is eighth grade












\[\left(\frac{c\,\Delta t}{2}\right)^{2} = d^{2} + \left(\frac{v\,\Delta t}{2}\right)^{2}\]
Solve for \(\Delta t\), use \(\Delta\tau = 2d/c\):

\[\Delta t = \frac{\Delta\tau}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}} = \gamma\,\Delta\tau\]

title: Time Dilation
text:
Meet \(\gamma\)











\(\gamma \geq 1\) always — flat and useless below \(0.1c\), vertical as \(v \to c\). Both regimes matter today.

title: Time Dilation
text:
Your lab partner flies past at \(0.8c\). Each of you carries an identical clock. You measure her clock ticking slow.
What does she measure about your clock?
(a) It ticks fast
(b) It ticks at the normal rate
(c) It ticks slow
(d) It depends on which of you accelerated in the past

title: Time Dilation
section: Both see the other slow. That is not a contradiction
text:
Both see the other slow. That is not a contradiction









Rating her clock takes two of yours — one where she starts, one where she ends. She answers: those two were never synchronized (Thursday!).

Each comparison uses a different pair of clocks. No clock is ever caught disagreeing with itself.

title: Time Dilation
section: Light does not get a clock
text:
Light does not get a clock









photon
massive object (you, a muon)




speed
\(c\), always
anything but \(c\)


rest frame
none

none — no clock ticks
ticks between any two events


needs \(\gamma\)?
no
yes




The light clock works because light carries no clock of its own — the photon is the ruler, never the thing being timed.

title: Time Dilation
text:
The muon









what
the electron’s heavy sibling — 207 × the mass, same charge


born
cosmic-ray collisions ~15 km up, at \(v \approx 0.995c\)


dies
\(\mu \to e + \nu + \bar{\nu}\) — always, no exceptions


lifetime
\(\tau = 2.2\ \mu\text{s}\) (mean — next slide!), on its own wristwatch
















Discovered 1936 — in this same cosmic rain, before any accelerator existed. So unexpected that I. I. Rabi asked: “Who ordered that?”

title: Time Dilation
section: An average, not an alarm clock
text:
An average, not an alarm clock










\(N = N_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\) — no fuse, the same dice every instant. \(\tau = 2.2\ \mu\)s is the mean, not a deadline.

title: Time Dilation
section: It should never reach the floor
text:
It should never reach the floor


distance light-speed allows a 2.2 us clock:  c*tau = 660 m
distance it must cover:                              15000 m
fraction surviving 15 km classically:  e^(-15000/660) = 1.3e-10



Newton’s verdict: about one muon in ten billion survives. The measured rain says otherwise — they arrive in droves.

title: Time Dilation
text:
Time dilation saves it


gamma at 0.995c                = 10.0
lab-frame mean lifetime        = 22 us
decay length gamma*beta*c*tau  = 6.6 km
surviving 15 km:  e^(-15/6.6) = 10%



In your frame the muon’s clock runs slow by \(\gamma \approx 10\). Its 2.2 μs stretch to 22 μs — and one in ten arrives. That is the rain.

title: Time Dilation
text:
They checked, twice









where
found




Rossi & Hall, 1941
Echo Lake, CO → Denver
muon loss with altitude fits \(\gamma\tau\), not \(\tau\)


Frisch & Smith, 1963
Mt. Washington → sea level
filmed it: survival ~13× the classical prediction





Thursday’s activity: Frisch–Smith’s actual count rates, and you run both calculations — one in each frame.

title: Time Dilation
text:
First job as a pair

How much does motion cost YOU? With your pair, compute \(\gamma - 1\) (use \(\gamma - 1 \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\beta^{2}\) for small \(\beta\)) for:

an airliner, \(v = 250\) m/s
the ISS, \(v = 7.7\) km/s
a GPS satellite, \(v = 3.9\) km/s

Then turn each into time lost per day of flight (86 400 s). One phone calculator per pair; one page, both names, keep it.

title: Time Dilation
text:
What you just computed


                v (m/s)     gamma-1     per day
airliner            250     3.5e-13     0.03 us
ISS                7700     3.3e-10    28.50 us
GPS satellite      3900     8.5e-11     7.31 us



Nobody ever felt time dilation. Below \(10^{-4}c\), \(\gamma - 1\) is parts per billion — which is why it took until 1905 to notice it in principle, and until 1941 to see it.

title: Time Dilation
section: And yet clocks are now good enough
text:
And yet clocks are now good enough


Hafele–Keating, 1971. Four cesium clocks flown around the world on airliners, then compared with the ones left home.



direction

title: Time Dilation
text:
Where it bites: GPS, again


Satellite clocks run slow by ~7 μs/day from their orbital speed — your pair just computed it.
Uncorrected, that is ~2 km of position error per day, growing.





Gravity speeds them up by ~45 μs/day — bigger, opposite sign. That story is general relativity; we point at it in L14.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Two observers moving relative to each other cannot agree about distances and times.
Fine. But before we can say how they disagree —

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
80% of you said \(c\) and \(c\)










“Light is always \(c\), so it must be \(c\) for both.” The first half is right.



(b) — pilot measures \(c\); in your frame the gap grows at \(0.1c\).

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Count it out, in your frame
text:
Count it out, in your frame
After 1 second, measured by you:










The gap opened by 0.1 light-seconds in 1 second. That is a rate of \(0.1c\) — and the pulse still moved a full light-second.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: The same thing, without any light
text:
The same thing, without any light

Two cars leave a junction in opposite directions, each at 60 mph.


The distance between them grows at 120 mph —
but no car broke the speed limit.



Nobody thinks 120 mph is a speed of a car. Same logic, same mistake.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Speed of what, measured by whom?
text:
Speed of what, measured by whom?


Always \(c\)
The pulse, measured by the pilot.
The pulse, measured by you.
Any light beam, any inertial frame.

Not a speed of light
The gap between rocket and pulse: \(0.1c\) in your frame.
Two beams fired apart: the gap closes at \(2c\) in your frame.



Nothing travels at \(0.1c\) or \(2c\) here. A gap is not an object.



Both of you measure the pulse itself at exactly \(c\) — even though one of you chases it at \(0.9c\). So what has to give?

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
What you predicted this morning
Prep check 1: name one everyday intuition that must break. 18 of you answered.











Half of you named time. That is the right instinct — and it is not the thing that breaks first.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Two of you went further



“Either the distance or the time variable has to change.”



“You would not be able to meet the family or friends you used to know.”



The first one has the whole argument in a sentence: \(v = d/t\), and if \(v\) is nailed down, something else has to give.



Today: what exactly is the \(d\), and what exactly is the \(t\)?

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Today is unglamorous and load-bearing
No paradoxes. No twins. No \(E = mc^2\).
Instead: what does it actually mean to measure when and where something happened?


Every argument in the next five weeks runs on the machinery built today. The students who find simultaneity confusing in two weeks are almost always the ones who skipped this.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
An event

An event is a single happening at a single place at a single moment.



Four numbers: \((t, x, y, z)\)

Two particles collide
A clock reads noon
Light reaches a detector
A firecracker’s first flash













“A firecracker explodes” is not an event — milliseconds, centimetres.



Also not events: “the train” (an object, not a happening) · “3 pm” (a time, no place) · “the collision was elastic” (a description, not a happening).

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: What a reference frame is not
text:
What a reference frame is not

A frame is not a point of view.
A frame is not where somebody is standing.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
What a reference frame is
A latticework of rulers and synchronized clocks, filling all of space.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Why this construction matters


Naive picture
One observer, one clock, watching from a distance.
Must correct for light travel time.
Confuses seeing with happening.

Latticework
Clocks everywhere, each recording locally.
No corrections needed.
Data collected afterward at leisure.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Now the hard part
The lattice needs its clocks synchronized.

Two clocks, 300 m apart. How do you set them to the same time?


You cannot carry one to the other — moving a clock changes what it reads, as we will see in L05. You need a signalling method, and every signal takes time.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Einstein synchronization









Flash a light at the midpoint. When it arrives, set both clocks to the same reading.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
You synchronize two clocks 300 m apart using a flash at the midpoint. Your friend, moving past at \(0.6c\), watches you do it.
Does your friend agree the clocks are synchronized?
(a) Yes — the procedure is symmetric
(b) No — she says one was set too early
(c) Only if she is also at the midpoint
(d) The question is meaningless

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: How fast is light, and how would you know?
text:
How fast is light, and how would you know?

Galileo tried it. Two lanterns, two hilltops, two assistants, and a shutter.
He concluded only that light is “if not instantaneous, extraordinarily rapid.”


What would you need, to do better?

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Rømer, 1676 — the first number


Jupiter’s moon Io eclipses on a strict schedule.
Except it runs late when Earth is far from Jupiter, and early when close.





  Extra distance across Earth's orbit : 2.992e+11 m
  Accumulated delay Rømer measured    : 22 minutes

  → c ≈ 2.267e+08 m/s
    modern value  2.998e+08 m/s   (about 24% low)

  Wrong by a quarter — and it settled the question that mattered:
  light does not arrive instantly.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Bradley, 1728 — aberration
Starlight arrives tilted — Earth moves while the light comes down.


Like running through vertical rain: you tilt the umbrella forward.



  tilt ≈ 20.5 arcsec
  c = v/tan(θ)
    ≈ 2.996e+08 m/s







Bradley’s value was within about 1% — far better than Rømer’s, and from an effect nobody was looking for.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Fizeau and Foucault — bringing it to the lab
text:
Fizeau and Foucault — bringing it to the lab



Fizeau, 1849 — toothed wheel
8 km to a mirror and back. 313,300 km/s


Foucault, 1850 — rotating mirror
Better precision — then light in water.



Light is slower in water — Newton’s corpuscles required faster.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Michelson made it his life’s work
text:
Michelson made it his life’s work


1879 — rotating mirror, improved · 299,910 ± 50 km/s
1926 — Mt. Wilson to Mt. San Antonio, 35 km baseline · 299,796 ± 4 km/s





He was still refining the measurement when he died in 1931. The 1926 value is within 4 km/s of the modern one — a relative error of about \(10^{-5}\).

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
1983 — the question dissolves

The metre is now defined as the distance light travels in \(1/299{,}792{,}458\) of a second.

So \(c = 299{,}792{,}458\) m/s — exactly, by definition, with no uncertainty.
You can no longer measure the speed of light.
You measure lengths with it.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
The catch nobody mentions
Every method on the last five slides measured a round trip.

Rømer — light out to Earth, but timed against a periodic source
Fizeau, Foucault, Michelson — out to a mirror, and back
Modern interferometry — out and back


We have never measured the one-way speed of light.


So why not put a clock at each end and time it one way?

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Convention, not ignorance
Einstein’s response: define the one-way speed to be \(c\) in both directions.


That is exactly what the midpoint-flash synchronization does — it assumes the two paths take equal time.




Not a gap in the theory. Every experimental prediction is unchanged whatever convention you adopt. But it is a choice, and knowing it is a choice is part of understanding what the theory claims.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Why not just carry a clock over?
text:
Why not just carry a clock over?

The obvious answer to synchronization: set two clocks side by side, then walk one of them 300 m down the track.


This fails — and how it fails is the subject of L05.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
You are the lattice

Everyone: phone out → time.ms. You are a lattice point.
Read your Time Offset — in milliseconds — and the round-trip delay.
Predict first — write it in your notebook, before we compare:

Your neighbours’ offsets match yours — yes or no?
If they differ, by how many ms? More or less than the time light needs to cross this room?




Then we read offsets down each row. Report your own clock — not the one at the front.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Three things a frame is not
text:
Three things a frame is not


Not a person
Nobody has to be watching. The lattice records whether or not anyone reads it.

Not a place
It fills all of space. There is no “where” the frame is.

Not a view
It measures. It does not see.


So — where is the train’s frame?



“The frame of the train” means the lattice that moves with the train — clocks at every point, all along the track and beyond, at rest relative to the train.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Reading the lattice: a worked case
text:
Reading the lattice: a worked case
A firecracker’s first flash — one event. Three lattice clocks are nearby.








Clock

The event’s time is \(t = 12.000000\) s. Read off \(C_1\) — the clock that was there.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
A number for the sceptics
Light covers 30 cm in one nanosecond.


Across this room (10 m): 33 ns
Buffalo to New York (470 km): 1.6 ms
Earth to Moon: 1.3 s




Grace Hopper handed out 30 cm wires and called them nanoseconds. It is still the best way to make \(c\) feel finite rather than infinite.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Where this leaves us


Settled today
An event is a happening: \((t,x,y,z)\)
A frame is rulers + synchronized clocks
Each event is read off the local clock
Synchronization is a definition

Open until Thursday
Does a moving observer agree the lattice is synchronized?
You voted. Most of you said no.
You were right — and it costs more than you think.

text:
Two experiments, one instrument



1887 · Cleveland 11 m folded arms ### Found nothing


2015 · Hanford & Livingston 4 km arms ### Found something

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Sound waves travel through air.
Ocean waves travel through water.
Waves on a string travel through the string.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Maxwell, 1865



James Clerk Maxwell 1831–1879


“We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.”
— A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field, 1865

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
The equations


Differential
\(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=\rho/\varepsilon_0\)
\(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0\)
\(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t\)
\(\nabla\times\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\mathbf{J}+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial\mathbf{E}/\partial t\)

Integral — the form from PHY 107
\(\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{A}=Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\)
\(\oint\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{A}=0\)
\(\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}=-\,d\Phi_B/dt\)
\(\oint\mathbf{B}\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}=\mu_0 I+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt\)


In vacuum these give a wave equation with speed \(c=1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}\)



From electricity and magnetism alone:  c = 299,792,458 m/s
Fizeau's 1849 measurement of light:    c = 313,300,000 m/s

Maxwell was not looking for light. It fell out.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
But a wave in what?



Wave
Medium
Speed set by




String
the string
tension, linear density


Sound
air
bulk modulus, density


Ocean
water
depth, gravity


Light
???
\(\varepsilon_0,\ \mu_0\)




\(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\mu_0\) are the electric and magnetic properties of something.



A fair objection: \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\mu_0\) are artefacts of SI. In Gaussian units both are 1 and \(c\) appears directly. But that only moves the question — something still sets the speed, and in 1865 nobody could say what.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
The luminiferous ether
To carry light, it must be:

Everywhere — all of space, Sun to Earth included
Enormously stiff — transverse waves at \(3\times10^{8}\) m/s means stiffer than steel
Frictionless — no measurable drag on planetary orbits over centuries
Invisible, massless, undetectable by any direct means



This should bother you. It bothered them too — but a wave propagating through nothing was worse.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
section: The ether was not a fringe idea
text:
The ether was not a fringe idea
It was the foundation of 19th-century optics — not idle metaphysics.



Young
1801
interference demands a wave


Fresnel
1818
diffraction and polarization explained


Bradley
1727
stellar aberration



Every one was read in ether terms, and the readings worked.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Young, 1801






“The middle of the two portions is always light, and the bright stripes on each side are at such distances that the light coming to them from one of the apertures must have passed through a longer space than that which comes from the other by an interval which is equal to the breadth of one, two, three, or more of the supposed undulations.”
— Young, Bakerian Lecture, 1803



Young’s own figure. Two sources; dark bands where they cancel.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Fresnel, 1818



1788–1827

Took the wave theory and made it quantitative — diffraction, polarization, the whole apparatus of 19th-century optics.
His ether was a mechanical, elastic solid.



Poisson objected that Fresnel’s theory absurdly required a bright spot at the centre of a circular shadow. Arago looked. The spot was there.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Bradley, 1727 — aberration



1693–1762


Starlight arrives tilted, because Earth moves while the light comes down.



Remember this one. On Thursday it closes off an escape route.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
The ether wind


If the ether is at rest and Earth orbits through it at 30 km/s, then from Earth’s frame there is a wind of ether streaming past.
Light should travel at \(c+v\) downwind, \(c-v\) upwind — like sound in moving air.






Earth's orbital speed:      v = 29,800 m/s
Ratio:                    v/c = 9.94e-05
Effect on travel time:  (v/c)² = 9.88e-09

A one-part-in-a-hundred-million effect.
No clock in 1887 could do that. No ruler could do that.



Aberration — the same effect that later ruled out ether drag.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
A swimmer moves at speed \(c\) relative to the water. A river flows at speed \(v\).

Swimmer A swims 100 m downstream, then back.
Swimmer B swims 100 m across, then back.

Who returns first?
(a) A    (b) B    (c) They tie    (d) Depends on \(v\)

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
section: Why the river matters going across
text:
Why the river matters going across
She cannot aim straight across — the current would carry her downstream.
She must aim upstream and let the current push her back onto the line.












Only \(\sqrt{c^2-v^2}\) is left for actually crossing.

The river costs her both ways — just less than it costs the downstream swimmer.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Downstream and back — the derivation
Each leg is just distance over speed. Only the speed relative to the bank changes.
\[t_\parallel=\underbrace{\frac{L}{c+v}}_{\text{with the current}}
            +\underbrace{\frac{L}{c-v}}_{\text{against it}}\]

Common denominator \((c+v)(c-v)=c^2-v^2\):
\[t_\parallel=\frac{L(c-v)+L(c+v)}{c^2-v^2}=\frac{2Lc}{c^2-v^2}\]


Divide top and bottom by \(c^2\):
\[t_\parallel=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{1-v^2/c^2}\]

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Across and back — the derivation
Effective crossing speed is \(\sqrt{c^2-v^2}\) — from the triangle.
Both legs are the same, so:
\[t_\perp=\frac{2L}{\sqrt{c^2-v^2}}\]

Factor \(c^2\) out of the square root:
\[\sqrt{c^2-v^2}=c\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\]


\[t_\perp=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\]

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Same prefactor, different power
\[t_\parallel=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{1-v^2/c^2}
\qquad
t_\perp=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\]
Write \(\beta^2 = v^2/c^2\). Then the bracket is \((1-\beta^2) < 1\), and
\[\frac{t_\parallel}{t_\perp}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\;>\;1\]

\[t_\parallel > t_\perp \quad \text{always}\]

The downstream gain never compensates the upstream loss.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
With numbers
\(L = 100\) m · swims at \(c = 2\) m/s · river \(v = 1\) m/s



Downstream
\(100/(2+1)\)
33.3 s


Back upstream
\(100/(2-1)\)
100.0 s




133.3 s


Across and back
\(200/\sqrt{3}\)
115.5 s





In still water both are 100 s. The river costs the parallel swimmer 33 s and the perpendicular swimmer 15 s — it hurts both, unequally.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Always, at every speed











The gap grows with speed, but it never closes — and it never changes sign.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Albert A. Michelson



1852–1931


Naval officer, then physicist
Obsessive about the speed of light — a career’s work
First American Nobel laureate in the sciences, 1907



“The more important fundamental laws and facts of physical science have all been discovered, and these are now so firmly established that the possibility of their ever being supplanted in consequence of new discoveries is exceedingly remote.”
— Michelson, 1894

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
…and Edward Morley



1838–1923

A chemist, not a physicist — and among the most precise experimentalists alive.
He had spent years measuring the atomic weight of oxygen to one part in ten thousand.



The experiment carries both names because it needed both skills: Michelson’s optics and Morley’s obsessive metrology.

Where we left off

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Today

A machine sensitive enough to feel a footstep — on this bench
What that machine said in 1887, in Cleveland
The tidy story of what happened next — and why it is wrong
Two sentences from 1905 that replace all of it

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
1881: the first try






Berlin, Helmholtz’s lab. Michelson is a 28-year-old US Navy officer on leave.
Arms \(L \approx 1.2\) m → predicted shift 0.04 fringes
Berlin traffic drowned the fringes → moved to a cellar in Potsdam. Stamping on the pavement 100 m away still shifted them.
Result: nothing. And nobody was convinced.



The instrument was paid for by Alexander Graham Bell.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
The machine they built, 1887




A 1.5-ton sandstone slab, floating on liquid mercury.
Why floating? So it can rotate without vibration.
Mirrors fold the light path to \(L = 11\,\mathrm{m}\) per arm.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Michelson interferometer

Watch the fringes move when I tap the table.
Write your prediction — in the notebook, before we rotate.
Rotate 90°.
See what the ether predicted — same rotation, in simulation.
Reconcile what you predicted with what happened.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What they measured, 1887

Dashed = the ether prediction, already reduced to one-eighth scale. Solid = what they measured.
Behind this figure: about six hours of data, over four days in July 1887.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
In their own words





“The Experiments on the relative motion of the earth and ether have been completed and the result decidedly negative.”
— Michelson to Lord Rayleigh, August 1887

He considered the experiment a failure, and moved on to other work.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
section: “The most famous failed experiment in history”
text:
“The most famous failed experiment in history”
It was not a failure.
Michelson himself was disappointed — he considered it a failure for years.
He was wrong about his own result.

A null result from an instrument sensitive enough to have seen the effect is a discovery.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What became of it






1907 — America’s first science Nobel: “for his optical precision instruments…” The ether experiment is not mentioned.
1902–04 — Morley and Miller do the seasonal repeats, bigger. Null.
1920s — Miller, alone on Mount Wilson, claims a positive signal.
1955 — traced to temperature gradients. Modern repeats: null, to parts in \(10^{18}\).



“Without your work, this theory would today be scarcely more than an interesting speculation.”
— Einstein, toasting Michelson, January 1931




Caltech, January 1931 — Michelson, Einstein, Millikan. Michelson died four months later.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What a null result destroys
No detectable ether wind — so something in the chain that predicted 0.4 fringes is false. There are only three ways out:

1. “Earth drags the ether along with it.” Then there is no wind at ground level, and the fringes rightly stay put. ✗ But dragged ether would also carry starlight along — and stellar aberration (Bradley’s tilted telescopes, from Tuesday) exists only if Earth moves through an undisturbed ether. One escape, two contradictory experiments.


2. “Motion through the ether squeezes the arms.” FitzGerald (1889) and Lorentz (1892): if the along-wind arm contracts by exactly \(\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\), the two delays cancel and the null is explained. ad hoc — a factor invented to erase this one experiment, with no mechanism and no independent prediction. But hold onto that factor: it is nearly right, for entirely different reasons — week 4.


3. “There is no ether.” Light needs no medium, and \(c\) is the same in every inertial frame. Einstein, 1905 — the only escape that predicts new physics instead of explaining away old data.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Here is the story every documentary and most textbooks tell:
Michelson–Morley destroyed the ether — so Einstein invented relativity.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Einstein, 1905




Bern, Switzerland. Age 26.

Not a professor. A patent examiner, third class.
Reviews patent applications — many for electromagnetic devices and clock synchronization.
In one year, 1905, publishes four papers. Any one of them would have made a career.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What Einstein actually wrote





“It is known that Maxwell’s electrodynamics — as usually understood at the present time — when applied to moving bodies, leads to asymmetries which do not appear to be inherent in the phenomena.”
— Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper, opening sentence, 1905




Not a word about Michelson–Morley. The paper mentions “unsuccessful attempts to discover any motion of the earth relative to the light medium” only in passing, a paragraph later.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
The asymmetry that bothered him


Magnet moves, coil at rest
Changing \(\mathbf{B}\) → induced electric field → current flows

Coil moves, magnet at rest
Charges move through \(\mathbf{B}\) → force \(q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\) → current flows


Same current. Same experiment. Two completely different explanations.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Two postulates

1. The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame.
2. The speed of light in vacuum is the same in every inertial frame, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer.


The first is old — Galileo would have signed it.
The second is the radical one.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Postulate 1 is 273 years older





“Shut yourself up with some friend in the main cabin below decks on some large ship … have the ship proceed with any speed you like, so long as the motion is uniform … You will discover not the least change in all the effects named, nor could you tell from any of them whether the ship was moving or standing still.”
— Galileo, Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, 1632

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
A rocket flies away from you at \(0.9c\) and fires a laser pulse straight ahead, in its direction of motion.
How fast does the pulse pull away from the rocket —
as measured by the pilot?  ·  as reckoned in your frame?
(a) \(c\) and \(c\)    (b) \(c\) and \(0.1c\)
(c) \(0.1c\) and \(c\)    (d) \(0.1c\) and \(0.1c\)

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Something has to give
Speed is \(\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}\).
If everyone measures the same speed for light, but they are moving relative to each other…

then they cannot agree about distance and time

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
The exchange rate







We keep
We give up




The laws of physics, identical for everyone
Absolute simultaneity


The speed of light, identical for everyone
Absolute time intervals


Causality · the spacetime interval
Absolute lengths · the ether

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Hendrik Lorentz




Wrote down the transformation equations (1892–1904) — before Einstein.
Believed length contraction was a real physical compression of matter moving through the ether.


“The chief cause of my failure was my clinging to the idea that the variable \(t\) only can be considered as the true time, and that my local time \(t'\) must be regarded as no more than an auxiliary mathematical quantity.”
— Lorentz, The Theory of Electrons, 1915 edition

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Henri Poincaré




Argued simultaneity is a convention. Saw the group structure. And in September 1904 — a year early — said this:


“… the principle of relativity, according to which the laws of physical phenomena should be the same, whether for an observer fixed, or for an observer carried along in a uniform movement of translation.”
— Poincaré, address at St. Louis, September 1904

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
So why Einstein?
Lorentz had the mathematics. Poincaré had the principle, and the name.

They had the mathematics. Einstein supplied the meaning: no ether, no mechanism — just two postulates and the courage to follow them.

Tuesday
Events, frames, and clocks
If observers disagree about time and distance, we had better be precise about what it means to measure either one.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Where the notebooks stand



Prediction
Landing. Almost everyone commits to something before the demo runs.

Observation
Strong. Particulars, sketches, first-attempt-vs-second.

Reconciliation
Strongest of the three. And usually the hardest to keep doing.




The part that does the learning is the part you did best.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
section: The trap: when your prediction was right
text:
The trap: when your prediction was right

A prediction that matches feels finished. It is not.
The template still asks: what would have made it come out differently?



“A different material.”



That answers a question nobody asked. The real one: which of my assumptions did this demo actually test?

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
section: What a good entry looks like
text:
What a good entry looks like

The strongest entry was not the one that was right.
It was the one whose prediction was falsifiable in a useful way.



“Refraction shouldn’t change once the table is done turning.”



That sentence forces you to watch during and after as separate events. It decides in advance what would count as being wrong.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
section: So your prediction was right. Now what?
text:
So your prediction was right. Now what?

You predicted no change. There was no change. Section 3 is not finished.




Instead of “nothing to reconcile”



Ask: what else would have produced exactly what I saw?




Tapping the table changed the pattern. Turning it did not.
So which did I actually test — the ether, or the table?

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Two lightning bolts strike the ends of a train.
You are on the platform. Your friend is on the train.
You say the strikes were simultaneous. Your friend says they were not.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
section: Same apparatus. Same room. Different reports.
text:
Same apparatus. Same room. Different reports.



“The pattern did not change after moving 90°.”


“It appeared to change the first time but did not.”



“The pattern changed and fluctuated while it moved.”


“Changed during the rotation, different after.”




Nobody misreported. Every one of these is correct.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
The question worth stealing


“What if there is ether — but it just never gets windy?”



The Earth moves at \(30\) km/s. And in December it moves the other way.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Tuesday’s question, unresolved
You synchronized two clocks with a flash at the midpoint.
Your friend, moving at \(0.6c\), said one was set too early.

Today: she is right. And so are you.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
What Tuesday gave us


A frame is a lattice of rulers and synchronized clocks.
Each event is recorded by the local clock.
Synchronization is a definition: midpoint flash, equal paths.




Everything today is these three facts plus the second postulate. No new machinery.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
The train









Lightning strikes both ends. Both of you are at the midpoint when it happens.







The strikes are events: one instant, one point at each end of the train.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Your account (platform)
Light from A and light from B each travel half the train’s length to reach you.
Equal distances. Equal speeds.

The two flashes reach you at the same instant.
You conclude: simultaneous.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Her account (train)
She is moving toward B and away from A.









The light from B has less ground to cover. It arrives first.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Both are right


Platform
Flashes arrive together Equal distances → simultaneous

Train
B arrives first Equal distances → B struck first


There is no fact of the matter about which came first.


“But what REALLY happened?” — the question has no answer, any more than “which end of this train is really the front?”

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
A new kind of picture

Stop drawing space. Start drawing space and time together.











Sitting still is a vertical line — you move through time, not space.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Light sets the scale











Choose units where \(c = 1\) — seconds and light-seconds — and light runs at exactly 45°. That choice is what makes the picture worth drawing.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
What “simultaneous” looks like











Simultaneous = level. One horizontal line is one moment of your time.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
The man who drew time




Hermann Minkowski (1864–1909) — Einstein’s mathematics professor at ETH Zürich.
September 1908, Cologne: “Space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows.”
Died four months later, at 44. Einstein first called the idea “superfluous learnedness” — then built general relativity on it.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Draw your own

Everyone, on paper — four of you at the board.

Axes: \(t\) up, \(x\) across. Units: seconds and light-seconds.
Your own worldline — you are sitting still.
A light flash from your position, both directions.
Mark one event: the door opens, now-ish, over there.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Two pictures, one light line











Draw hers into yours: her light line lands on yours — her axes do not.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Now watch it move — minkowski.html
Predict first: as \(v\) grows, does A or B become earlier — and does the gold light line move?

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Two events are spacelike separated — too far apart for light to travel between them.
Can an observer see them in reverse order?
(a) No — that would violate causality
(b) Yes, and it violates nothing
(c) Only for \(v > c\)
(d) Only if they are simultaneous in some frame

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Putting numbers on it
Train of proper length \(L = 300\) m, moving at \(v = 0.6c\).

Offset between the two strikes in her frame: \(\Delta t' = \dfrac{\gamma v L}{c^{2}}\)



gamma        = 1.2500
Delta t'     = 0.7505 microseconds
light covers = 225.0 m in that time

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
The scale of it



Speed
Offset across a 300 m train




30 m/s (a real train)
\(1.0\times10^{-13}\) s


0.001 \(c\)
\(1.0\times10^{-9}\) s


0.6 \(c\)
\(7.5\times10^{-7}\) s





The effect was always there. It only became visible when we built things that move fast, or clocks precise enough to see \(10^{-13}\) s.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text: The light cone

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Timelike, spacelike, lightlike


Timelike
Inside the cone.
A signal can connect them.
Time order is fixed — every frame agrees.

Spacelike
Outside the cone.
No signal can connect them.
Time order is frame-dependent.

Lightlike
On the cone.
Only light connects them.
Order fixed; separation zero.


Frames disagree about order only where disagreement cannot cause trouble.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
section: The objection you are all having
text:
The objection you are all having

“But she’s moving. Surely she should correct for that, and then she’d agree with the platform.”


There is nothing to correct. She is at rest in her own frame.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Two frames, side by side


Platform frame
The train is moving.
The platform lattice is synchronized.
The train’s clocks are not synchronized — the front one lags.

Train frame
The platform is moving.
The train lattice is synchronized.
The platform’s clocks are not synchronized — by the same rule.


Each says the other’s clocks are out of step. Both are correct.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Activity

Self-check with a partner — simultaneity
§II on the handout: Alan on the ground, Beth on the train, two sparks.
Do A (Alan’s frame), then B (Beth’s frame). Swap and mark.



Last chance to choose a partner — self-selection closes at the end of today. Work with someone you would want, then declare it before you leave.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
What today actually changed


You still have
Light at \(c\) in every frame
A lattice that measures cleanly
Agreement on what happens at an event
Causal order, wherever it matters

You have lost
A universal “now”
Frame-independent simultaneity
The idea that one frame is the real one

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Where this actually bites


GPS. Satellites move at ~3.9 km/s. Across the constellation the simultaneity offset runs to
\[\Delta t' = \frac{vL}{c^2} \approx 860\ \text{ns}\]













Ignore it and your position is wrong by about 260 m.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
section: And where it decides the physics
text:
And where it decides the physics


Particle colliders. LHC bunches cross every 25 ns — light moves 7.5 m in that time. Which collision happened “first” is frame-dependent; the detector timing must be defined, not assumed.

Neutrino timing, 2011. OPERA reported neutrinos arriving 60 ns early — apparently faster than light.
The error was a loose fibre-optic cable and a clock offset. A synchronization fault.



The claim survived six months of scrutiny before the cable was found. Nobody doubted the physics first — they doubted the clocks, and they were right to.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
What this costs Newton



Newton
Einstein




One universal time for everyone
Each frame has its own time


“Now” extends across the universe
“Now” is frame-dependent


Simultaneity is a fact
Simultaneity is a relation


Space and time independent
Mixed by motion





Newtonian time is not wrong — it is the \(v \ll c\) limit. At walking speed the disagreement between your “now” and a passing train’s “now” is about \(3\times10^{-15}\) seconds across a room.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Next week
